assumptions: The owner sets a price that customers accept and that covers the bundle's work.
The number and duration of appointments, including email, booking, setup, payment and follow-up, total no more than six staff hours.
Any consumables or materials remain within the EUR 120 one-off allowance.
Customers accept payment at completion and collect or attend as agreed.
evaluations.proposal: Sell a fixed-price minor-repair and tune-up bundle through a small set of pre-booked counter appointments, offered first-come to all forty opted-in customers, with payment at completion and a hard capacity cap.
evaluations.reason: The proposal uses only the existing counter, tools and opted-in email list, and its appointment cap can bound delivery within six hours and two weeks. However, it does not specify price, number or duration of appointments, preparation and follow-up time, or cash costs, so feasibility is conditional rather than demonstrated. Payment at completion is a weaker demand signal because the owner may perform work before receiving payment. Demand would be observable through completed paid bookings, with continuation based on reaching the cap profitably or stopping if bookings are insufficient. It is useful for customers needing routine repairs, but it tests the same value category as candidate 712dec and is therefore not materially distinct from it in service type.

assumptions: The recent-interaction records identify a relevant need without contacting non-opted-in customers.
The owner can process the capped number of bicycles within six additional hours.
Prepayment can be handled with existing tools and no recurring cost.
Materials and consumables stay within EUR 120.
Customers accept the stated price and drop-off and collection windows.
evaluations.proposal: Sell a fixed-price minor-repair and tune-up bundle during one or two defined drop-off windows, prioritising opted-in customers with a relevant recent shop interaction, requiring prepayment, and stopping at a stated revenue target or the two-week deadline.
evaluations.reason: Prepayment provides a clear paid demand signal before delivery, and targeted selection plausibly improves relevance while remaining within the forty opted-in customers. Drop-off windows can reduce handling overhead and the revenue cap supplies an observable stop condition. The proposal still omits the revenue target, price, number of bicycles, service durations, preparation, collection and follow-up time, and cash itemisation, so the six-hour and EUR 120 limits are not proven without a tightly chosen cap. Prioritisation also assumes the shop has a compliant way to identify relevant recent interactions. Like candidate 5a003, it tests a repair bundle rather than a materially different service value.

assumptions: Customers are available to participate during the drop-off or service window rather than merely leaving bicycles.
The owner can conduct the capped sessions, including preparation and follow-up, within six hours.
Existing tools suffice and materials cost no more than EUR 120.
Customers accept payment at session end and the proposed price.
The self-identified needs can be matched to a bicycle-care demonstration.
evaluations.proposal: Offer paid one-to-one bicycle-care demonstrations, selected from replies by all forty opted-in customers who identify a matching need, delivered through one or two drop-off windows, with payment at the end and a hard capacity cap.
evaluations.reason: This tests a materially different value proposition—customer learning rather than repair output—and self-identified needs can make the offer relevant. The capacity cap can bound work, and the email channel and existing counter/tools fit the stated resources. The drop-off arrangement is poorly aligned with a one-to-one demonstration: a drop-off and later collection may prevent the customer from attending the session, so access and fulfilment are unclear. Payment at the end also leaves demand less firmly confirmed before the owner's time is spent. No price, session length, place count, preparation, replies, setup, payment or follow-up estimates are supplied, so budget and six-hour feasibility remain conditional.

The proposal does not itemise price, materials, number or duration of appointments, email and follow-up effort, so it does not establish that the complete pilot fits EUR 120 and six hours; those limits require explicit conservative caps. The service is plausibly relevant but willingness to pay and response rate are unverified. It is materially different from the repair-bundle candidates in the kind of value sold, though the same general booking mechanism is used.

assumptions: The prioritised recent-repair customers are among the forty opted-in customers.

evaluations.proposal: Offer a fixed-price safety and maintenance check to opted-in customers with a relevant recent shop interaction, using a single email wave, deposit-backed counter appointments and no second outreach.
evaluations.reason: The single wave, opted-in recipient restriction and deposit requirement fit the stated resource and contact constraints. A small appointment set can be bounded to six hours and two weeks, and deposits provide a partial paid-demand signal before delivery. However, the candidate does not specify price, deposit, appointment count, service duration or cash itemisation, so feasibility and the continue-or-stop threshold remain conditional. The offer tests demand for preventive assessment rather than a repair outcome.

assumptions: The single clinic has enough individually booked places to produce useful evidence while remaining within six hours.
The clinic format is suitable for the repair bundle and existing tools can support simultaneous or sequential work.
Parts and consumables remain within EUR 120, with no recurring spending.
Customers accept a shared clinic format and prepayment.
evaluations.proposal: Offer a fixed-price minor-repair and tune-up bundle to opted-in customers who identify a matching need, delivering it in one short individually booked clinic with prepaid places and a capacity cap.
evaluations.reason: The clinic and capacity cap can concentrate setup and delivery within six hours, while prepayment confirms demand before the owner spends delivery time. The email audience and existing counter/tools comply with the resource and contact limits. Prices, clinic duration, number of places, materials and follow-up time are not supplied, so the required cash and staff-time fit is not demonstrated. The clinic arrangement is materially different from individual appointments, though the revenue offer and payment model overlap with candidate 1. Continue if prepaid places reach the defined threshold; otherwise stop after the capped clinic offer.

assumptions: The revenue target would be set low enough to prevent more than six total staff hours, although that limit is not expressed in the candidate.
The owner can safely and clearly deliver one-to-one instruction using the existing counter and tools.
Customers with recent repair interactions want instruction rather than completed repair work and will prepay.
Any materials used are one-off costs within EUR 120.
evaluations.proposal: Offer prepaid one-to-one bicycle-care instruction to relevant opted-in recent-repair customers, using one or two drop-off windows and running until a revenue target or the two-week deadline.
evaluations.reason: The skill session is a materially different educational service, and prepayment can confirm demand before delivery. The opted-in recipient restriction and existing tools fit the resources constraint. However, a revenue cap and two-week deadline do not cap the number or duration of sessions, and drop-off windows add handling and collection work; the proposal therefore does not guarantee compliance with the six-hour limit. It also lacks price, target, session duration, appointment count and materials itemisation. Demand would be measured by prepaid bookings, but the continue-or-stop rule is underspecified beyond the unquantified revenue target.

assumptions: The owner may set pilot prices and reserve limited service appointments.
Existing customers can understand and respond to a concise service offer by email.
Any materials purchased for a pilot are one-off costs and can be obtained within the EUR 120 allowance.
search_material.composition_guidance: Combine one paid service offer with one bounded delivery arrangement, one recipient-selection approach, one customer-commitment model and one explicit pilot boundary. Count email preparation, replies, booking, setup, delivery, payment handling and follow-up within the six-hour limit. Keep the three composed pilots materially different in the kind of value sold and the way paid demand is confirmed; do not create differences only through wording or price.

constraints.text: Spend at most EUR 120 in total, with no recurring spending commitment.
Use at most six additional staff hours including preparation, contact and delivery, and finish within two weeks.
Use existing tools and the counter; no new software, hires or paid advertising.
Contact only the forty customers who opted in, using the existing email channel.

search_material.context_summary: One owner runs the shop. The goal is to test paid demand with existing tools and customer relationships, without committing to a continuing programme.

criteria.text: Itemise cash and staff time and show that the complete pilot fits both limits.
State the paid demand signal, assumptions and an observable continue-or-stop decision.
Offer materially different ways to test additional revenue, not changes of wording.
Use only the existing tools, counter, email channel and available staff capacity, with no recurring commitment.
Define what the customer receives, how access is limited and when payment or agreement occurs.
Make the offer plausibly useful to existing customers while clearly labelling unverified willingness to pay and response assumptions.

dimensions.meaning: The paid service customers are invited to buy.

variants.text: A fixed-price safety and maintenance check covering inspection, adjustments and a short written recommendation.
A fixed-price bundle combining a common minor repair with a defined tune-up or adjustment.
A paid one-to-one bicycle care session in which the owner demonstrates maintenance tasks on the customer’s bicycle.

dimensions.meaning: How the shop limits and fulfils the service during the two-week pilot.

variants.text: Offer a small number of pre-booked counter appointments at set times.
Accept bicycles during one or two defined drop-off windows and complete the service by a stated collection time.
Run a single short clinic with several individually booked customer places, using the counter and existing tools.

dimensions.meaning: Which opted-in existing customers receive the offer or priority access.

variants.text: Email all forty opted-in customers with a capped first-come offer.
Prioritise customers whose recent shop interaction suggests a relevant maintenance need, while staying within the opted-in list.
Email all forty customers a short choice of service needs and allocate the limited offer to replies that match the pilot.

dimensions.meaning: What customer agreement confirms demand before the owner spends time delivering the service.

variants.text: Require payment when the customer books a reserved place.
Require a small deposit to reserve a place and collect the balance on completion.
Reserve places by email and charge only when the completed service is collected or the session ends.

dimensions.meaning: The explicit limit that keeps the experiment bounded while making its result observable.

variants.text: Set a maximum number of paid places and stop accepting bookings when they are filled.
Run the offer until a stated additional-revenue target or the two-week deadline is reached.
Send one offer wave, deliver only confirmed responses, and make no second outreach during the pilot.

facts: The shop has ordinary bicycle repair tools and a service counter.
Forty existing customers have opted in to service emails.
The owner can devote six additional staff hours over the next two weeks.
The total additional cash allowance is EUR 120.
search_material.objective: Propose three distinct two-week pilots through which a neighbourhood bicycle repair shop could earn additional service revenue from existing customers, within the stated cash and staff-time limits.
unknowns: Customer willingness to pay and response rate have not been measured.
The most attractive additional service category for these customers is unknown.
The number of appointments the owner can deliver within six additional hours is unknown.
